However, what Ndemic Creations has been doing since the start of the COVID pandemic merits a lot more than just a good review. Keeping the game updated and afloat besides being banned in China, donating part of their earnings to cure research efforts and now, raising awareness on key issues with their future "Save the World" update (which will be free until a vaccine for COVID is discovered).

Plague Inc is a rather satisfying simulation in which the player's goal is to infect and kill off the entire world. Just exactly how the player chooses to tackle this is up to them.

Gameplay

The player can choose to slowly infect the population, remaining undetected and non-lethal, and then strike once much of the world's population is infected by evolving lethality to kill fast and unexpectedly, making it difficult for the world to react and cure it in time or just try to kill the world as fast as possible which usually results in losing the game as many of the more isolated countries such as Greenland will shut their ports and airports making it very difficult to infect them.

Content

The player is not presented with just one disease type, but many. These disease types range from a neurax worm which allows the player to manipulate infected hosts to their advantage to the necroa virus which allows the player to unleash a devastating zombie apocalypse on the world. It doesn't stop here though as there is a rather extensive community workshop with countless unique diseases thanks to the scenario creator which is available to every player who owns the game.

More coming

The developers of this game are also working on a multiplayer mode which will see two players battle it out to see who's plague is superior. The game is also regularly updated with new content and bug fixes.

Conclusion

While Plague Inc is not perfect, it offers great replayability with different ways to beat different scenarios and higher difficulty modes which can really challenge the player. The price is rather steep so I would suggest waiting until the game is on sale to get the best value for money. 8/10 - Great game.

This is an odd one. 

It may seem ironic to recommend a game about wiping out humanity with deadly diseases in the middle of a pandemic, but beneath the surface and the stress-inducing concept, lies a simple game, a simple premise that is not overly complicated nor does it go out of its way to simulate pandemics. 

At its core, it's a clicker game with a steep learning curve and randomness thrown in the mix. It's a race against time; a strenuous exercise in patience. The premise of the game, your purpose, is to create a disease that wipes out humanity.  Pick a spot in the world, each with their own climates, population, economic strength, optimal means of transmission, etc, and start from there. The world will try to stop you so you must beat it to the punch. That is basically what the game revolves around.

The real appeal of the game, however, is in the progression system. A variety of unlocks that can make each game feel different, easier or even harder. Different pathogen types will impact how you approach your game as both unlocks and pathogen type will have their strengths and weaknesses which add to the tactical depth but also making the game highly replayable and improving the overall experience. 

Yes, it can be stressful as you are always up against the time. At higher difficulties you will really feel the tension. You planned meticulously, making the right choices, picking the right upgrades, or so you thought. Then you lose, those pesky humans finding a way to stop you, and more often that not, you end up being the master of your own demise, your choices having backfired yet it's too late to react. Losing is a rather essential part of the game; it's part of the progression. 

You may go in with the expectation that you'll create your disease the way [i]you[/i] want to, but you find yourself often focusing on survival. It is perfectly possible to 'simulate' the virtual Spanish flu, but your goal is to win. Unforeseen circumstances will have you changing tactics as you go, so you may find it difficult to play the role you wanted, per se. While it can be slightly frustrating, it does add to the realism factor. A double edged knife.

There is multiplayer and co-op modes. I haven't played PvP yet, but I am assuming it is not that much different to co-op, which is rather simplistic, with limited unlocks and no scenarios but it is an enjoyable, on-the-side experience. Destroy the world along with a friend, work together or sabotage each other.

Speaking of scenarios, there's a lot of fun and unique ones. Plenty more in the workshop. It's not all about wiping out the world either. Instead of a literal disease, you can play a scenario in which you spread figurative ones, such as [i]weebism[/i], where the world is transformed into anime-obsessed, manga-consuming, waifu-adoring, brainless weebs. 

I shudder at the thought.

At any rate, it is also worth recommending this game at the present time due to an upcoming update which will bring a feature I'd always hoped existed. The one missing thing: Saving the world from the clutches of a pandemic, allowing you save the world not just destroy it. A fitting addition that perfectly reflects the current situation of the world. 

Give it a shot.

[b]Plague Inc[/b] is a very unique game to me, as it blends horror with strategy; you play as a disease, and your job is to infect the entire world and kill everyone. A concept that scares me in a way, but makes for some fun gameplay. [b]Plague Inc[/b] has also just received a new DLC called [b]Aliens and Anti-Vaxxers[/b] at the time of writing this review, which brings in some new scenarios and content for the game.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The gameplay for [b]Plague Inc: Evolved[/b] has lots of depth to it and strategy for you to use in order to win. There are multiple disease types that you can use; you only have access to one at the start, and a few add-ons for the game. But you can unlock more as you beat the [b]plagues[/b] one by one on normal difficulty.

There are 12 different [b]plagues[/b] for you to use; each has a different way of infecting people and ways for people to combat it. For your [b]plague[/b] to evolve and kill people, you will need to put in some upgrades to make it stronger. These upgrades cost DNA, which you can get gradually or by popping red and orange bubbles, which will give you some.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3745443971 
Each [b]plague[/b] has a different play style and a strategy for you to beat it. I recommend trying to get transmissions first, so it can spread. You will get random [b]mutations[/b] for free on occasion, and you do have the option to keep them or devolve them if you have too many symptoms before infecting the whole world. Your [b]plague[/b] may get noticed early, and there is no way for you to win, depending on the [b]plague[/b]. This does, of course, depend on the [b]plague[/b] you choose. [b]Nano-Virus[/b], in particular, is a unique [b]plague[/b], as you notice from the start, and you must be aggressive to win.

However, I did mention that your objective is to wipe out humanity, so in return, humanity won’t like that, and they will try to fight you to stop you from spreading. They will also try to hinder or limit your ability to spread, and you will have to use DNA points on things like drug resistance, air and water travel, and [b]genetic hardening[/b] to help slow down research and cure speed.

You also have to keep an eye on sea and air ports, as these are your best ways to spread your plague. Countries will close their air and sea ports to stop the spread, and if that happens, it can be extremely difficult for the [b]disease[/b] to spread, or outright impossible. [b]Greenland[/b] in particular only has a seaport, and if they close their seaport and you haven’t infected them, your run is over, depending on your plague. [b]Fungus[/b] can spread by spores and is airborne, so it can reach other countries that way, and the [b]Xenolith crystal[/b] has multiple ways to win with it.

Your [b]plague[/b] will also get different reactions in different countries, and they will respond in a variety of ways that can both hinder and help you from spreading. Paying attention to the events of the world can be very helpful, as it will help you get a game plan on what you need in order to win with your disease.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3745443480
You will also want to spend some of your DNA on some symptoms. You will need to be careful about what symptoms you get, as if you have too many, your plague will be discovered. If you get discovered too early, especially on the higher difficulties, it may make your run extremely difficult or impossible to win. You also need to be careful about your lethality as well. If you kill all of your hosts before infecting everyone, you can lose the game that way too. You will also want to spend some DNA on some abilities like cold, heat, and drug resistance. You will need to get some drug resistance so you can increase your infectivity in richer countries.

You can also get some transmission, like air or water transmission, to help spread your disease. This is important as plans and boats will install filters that will prevent it from spreading, and if, let's say, some places do close their borders, you can still infect them with things like livestock, birds, insects, or blood. Unless it’s an island, where that may be a bit more difficult, unless, as mentioned before, you are playing as Fungus, as it spreads by spores.

Some of my favorite plagues to play as include the [b]Nano-virus[/b], with its aggressive playstyle. [b]Fungus[/b] can be very fun with its unique way of spreading, and the recent DLC released with the [b]Xenolith crystal[/b], where you turn Earth and everyone into a green crystal.

There is also a [b]Cure mode[/b], where you fight to save the world from a pandemic. It’s a new way to play the game, and it’s also difficult, as you need to not only fight the disease but also keep your public global authority up as well. If you lose your reputation, it’s game over, or if humanity dies out. There is heavy micromanagement, balancing resources, and political compliance, which are the few things that you have to worry about.

I haven’t really touched [b]Cure Mode[/b] much, so I can’t really say much about it, but it is a fun, different way to play [b]Plague Inc. Evolved[/b]. There are also costume scenarios, where you can play as a costume disease from the community workshop. However, there are also a few official scenarios made by the devs that you can play.

[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]
[b]Plague Inc: Evolved[/b] is a fun strategy game that has a good amount of content for the 19.49 CAD that it’s worth. The only thing that I would point out about the game is that there isn’t a whole lot of room for creativity in the game. As this is a strategy game, on the higher difficulties, you have to kind of play a certain way, or winning is just impossible. But other than that, Plague Inc: Evolved is a fun strategy game for those who like them.

I have been bittersweet about Plague Inc. for years, because instead of being an actual simulator, it's more like a puzzle: your task is to find the one strategy that consistently works, and it's often very counter-intuitive. Once you find that strategy, you're pretty much set and can consistently win with any disease type. I came back to Plague inc. for The Cure expansion (which is being offered for free for the time being) hoping the game design had finally improved.

Spoiler alert: it didn't. Everything in the gameplay of this expansion is out of whack. For example: If the pandemic gets out of control and starts infecting and killing people massively, you can supposedly quarantine the whole continent. Good luck with that though: several countries will rebel, with quarantine non-compliance rates easily reaching 100% even with all the noncompliance-mitigation upgrades bought (e.g. giving people financial aid so they can stay home without losing money). How realistic is it that NO ONE in an entire country would listen to the government, even though everyone around them is dying like flies?

Another example: there is now Authority mechanic, where if your Authority reaches zero you lose because no one respects you anymore as a world leader. It is good on paper, but the way it's currently implemented is just idiotic. Even if the infection and mortality rates are going down and you're implementing new anti-pandemic measures all the time, you still bleed Authority like crazy. So apparently the player  loses the game for "not being a competent world leader" even though the pandemic is being effectively controlled and the situation is improving, with a vaccine 70% on the way to distribution? Ludicrous.

Reading the game's forums, people have found a (unintuitive) strategy that works for every disease type, which is to lockdown the continent the disease spawns in as soon as possible and ignore upgrades that reduce the disease infectivity and mortality. This is arbitrary and doesn't make sense. Several have claimed that you can just use this same strategy against all disease varieties (virus, bacteria, fungus etc.) and you will win. Again, this is not a simulator, this is a puzzle where the developers don't give you enough hints to solve it, and in fact, deliberately confuse you, and where a big part of the content only *pretends* to be of any use.

I'm done with giving this game any further chances, and will now get my disease-game fix from other games such as Bio Inc. Redemption, which I hope is better than this mess.

This was most enjoyed in the days of miniclip.com and shockwave games. This game was sort of ground breaking in the sense it wasn't anything I've seen before. Fast forward to today and the devs have successfully launched a few games on Steam. Although this can feel a little like a mobile game, it does have a certain progression that respects the player enough to give a challenge. In short, will recommend but on the same steep sale that I got it on.

Plague Inc: Evolved's [b]gameplay[/b] relies mostly on a point and click [b]control[/b] scheme. The main view for most of the game is a map of the world. The player essentially controls the view of the map, clicks the user interface to interact with the game. The game itself doesn't require much player interaction as its mostly observation. The game is essentially choosing a disease, naming it, watching it spread, mutating it as points accumulate, and popping notification bubbles that come up. I wish there was a little more interaction rather than popping random bubbles that appear on the map. These bubbles either give the player more DNA mutation points or slow the research against the disease. The player can't quite see the extent of their disease in any third or first person mode. Even though the game sounds very straight forward and not much is going on, there is a [b]gameplay[/b] loop that is addicting - especially with a campaign that introduces variances.

The [b]visuals and graphics[/b] are okay. There is some minor animation going on showing players where infections start and how they travel around (by boat or by plane). Messages sometimes randomly pop up informing the player of world events that are occurring, and if the player is good enough, can actually change the messages. For example, Brexit happening is a big one, and somehow through whatever I did, I mitigated and avoided the Brexit situation. The [b]sounds and music[/b] are also okay. They're not phenomenal, but they're at least present. I've actually turned down the this domain because the repetition of the same sounds can become annoying.

In short, I will sort of recommend this game, even if it's on a major sale. The campaign was well done - making an effort to familiarize the player with how to play the game, and sort of adds a new spin to each scenario. The biggest issue for me is staring at the same screen over and over, and simply playing whack-a-mole with my mouse. Really wish there was more interaction. The game does have a "sandbox" type mode and enough for the campaign, but once its done, don't see myself (personally) coming back often.

This is a decent game with quite a bit of content as far as game mechanics goes.  There's plenty of upgrades and different pathogens to choose from.  The issue comes from one giant flaw in my opinion; there's only one strategy that really works.  

The game is basically a race between your pathogen's ability to wipe out the humans, and their ability to cure it.  As soon as they notice the symptoms of your disease, they will begin to work on finding a cure.  This can happen very early on and the more people you infect/kill, the harder and more fervently the humans will work to cure it.  There are in-game "upgrades" you can purchase with your points to slow the humans, but they are laughably under-powered; reducing their progress bar by a measely 5-10% and costing you dearly in points. This might sound like a challenging mechanic to be conquered in an epic battle of wits, but it's not.  The gameplay is very limited as far as thwarting the humans or slowing them down, only offering a few one-time-use options for reducing their progress bar.  This is in leiu of the fact that should even one of the numerous island nations close their borders before they are infected, you just lost the entire game. This happens VERY often.  Unless, as I mentioned above, you use the strategy below.

The ONLY strategy I have found that really works is keeping your disease hidden from the humans by keeping it from presenting with any symptoms until 95%-100% of the population is infected.  You then use all of your banked points and flood them into symptoms until your disease is incredibly lethal, and then sit back and watch.  If this sounds boring, that's because it is.  You are literally just sitting there looking at a screen for 10 minutes clicking around a few times.  Pretty dissappointing for a game with so much potential.  

I really gave this one the old college try, but it retains its entertainment value for far less time than I spent playing it.  $15 is better spent elsewhere.

Typically a game like [I]Plague Inc.: Evolved[/I] would not get much of my attention. Yet, these are not typical times, and for better or worse, this game has garnered more interest than before. All the press that [I]PI:E[/I] received had my curiosity, and having played it, it got my full attention.

[B][U]But first, a preamble...[/U][/B]
I don’t think [I]PI:E[/I] is exploiting the crises, troubles and tragedies that COVID-19 has caused. After all, the original version of the game, named [I]Plague Inc.[/I], was first released on iOS and Android in 2012, and on Windows Phone in 2015. [I]PI:E[/I] is the remake of the original game. The PC, Xbox One and PlayStation 4 versions were released in 2015 – 2016, and the Nintendo Switch version in August 2019. All that happened at a time when pandemics only happened in entertainment, prior to the current realities.

Given that, [I]PI:E[/I] is not COVID-19 simulator, and it’s unfair to reduce this game to that label. I believe this game got the attention that it currently has because people are seeking ways to make sense of the chaos in our world, and they found it here. [I]PI:E[/I] offers a safe environment, in which people can confront their fears, and seek some control in these unpredictable times. It’s simple enough for people to visualize the Coles Notes or CliffNotes version of a possible, bleak outcome of this pandemic.

As a frontline staff helping with the management of the pandemic, I’ve come home from work feeling physically tired, emotionally drained, and utterly demoralized. I’ve found a cathartic release in playing [I]PI:E[/I], as morbid as it may seem. It’s my mental health therapy, though admittedly it may not be the best way to resolve my anxieties. At the same time, I understand that [I]PI:E[/I] is a game with a simplified simulation model that does not truly reflect the complex realities and relationships of biology, epidemiology, politics, commerce, as well as humanity’s resilience, ingenuity, and -- let’s face it -- stupidity.

[B][U]So having said that...[/U][/B]
I do find [I]PI:E[/I] fascinating, cathartic, and frightening. It’s fascinating because the developer has taken many variables into consideration when designing the simulation model that is the backbone of the game. It’s cathartic because I feel like I have some control over a pandemic when playing it. It’s frightening because I can visualize the global chaos that a rapidly evolving pathogen can cause in matter of game hours.

Yet in real life, pathogens do not dictate how they evolve and devolve. Evolution is a process that happens with a combination of chance mutations and survival of the fittest. [I]PI:E[/I] is a variation of world domination strategy games. You play as a pathogen attempting to conquer the world by evolving and devolving purposefully, so that you can maximize your pathogen’s potency by altering your levels of infectivity, severity and lethality.

You’d notice I’ve been using the word, “pathogen”, and not “virus” exclusively. That’s because the game allows you to control various real pathogens (i.e. bacterium, virus, fungus, parasite, and prion) and fictitious ones (i.e. Neurax Worm, Necroa Virus, Nano-Virus, Simian Flu, and Shadow Plague). Each pathogen has its strengths and weaknesses, forcing you to employ different strategies to conquer the world for different plagues. Pathogens can also be personalized at beginning of each game by modifying their various abilities via gene insertions.

Naming your pathogen is a fun part of [I]PI:E[/I]. You can be give your virus a serious name like “Neovid-01” (as I did), or give it a fun name like “Cyrus” (as I should have done). You can be erudite and call your deadly bacterium “Sicarium” and your zombie-making virus “Inferni Ambulans”. In my opinion, it’s more entertaining when pathogen names are silly (e.g. calling your mind-controlling worm “Swiggly Wiggly”) or cheeky (e.g. calling your parasite “BJH”).

At the normal difficulty setting, [I]PI:E[/I] is not very demanding at first. It gets more difficult when playing as a fungus and prion, and much more challenging as a Necroa Virus and other more advanced pathogens. Normal difficulty level is not that realistic as well, with only 67.3% of people washing their hands, doctors working only 3 days a week, and sick people being ignored. That’s not how to respond to a pandemic!

The game’s brutal and mega brutal difficulty levels are more like our real life right now, with people washing their hands compulsively, doctors investing in research and never going home, and random medical check-ups happening, etc. That’s why I stated earlier that it’s unfair reduce [I]PI:E[/I] as simply COVID-19 simulator. It’s a much more sophisticated game.

[I]PI:E[/I] gets a bit more complex when you play as the Simian Flu and Shadow Plague. These two fictional pathogens allow you to create armies of apes and vampires respectively. In these plagues, you’ll need to balance the infection of the pathogen, death of the infected, as well as rise of your apes or vampires. These two pathogens, as well as the other fictional ones, offer a bit of escape from the grim, real world.

The game also presents a slew of scenarios for you to play. Some:
[LIST]
[*]change the basic rules of the game (e.g. cold countries become hot; rich countries become poor; all countries have solid responses to outbreaks; people can teleport to the safest countries)
[*]are whimsical (e.g. using the mind-controlling worm to spread Christmas cheer; creating and distributing a board game, while making it a global bestseller), and
[*]offer informational “pathogens” to spread (e.g. Fake News, toxic ideologies).
[/LIST]
At the time of this review, the developer are said to be creating a play mode, in which you fight the COVID-19 pandemic.

[B][U]Final thoughts[/U][/B]
During anxious and uncertain times these days, [I]PI:E[/I] is not going to be for everyone, especially when it comes to playing as a killer virus at one point. However, playing [I]PI:E[/I] can be a cathartic and educational experience. Just as one have learned from [I]SimCity[/I] that residential properties near industrial areas have lower property value; and from [I]Civilization[/I] that you can defeat a tank with phalanx unit (hmm...wait), one can learn from [I]PI:E[/I] some factors that can trigger or hinder a pandemic.

Whether you end up trying [I]PI:E[/I] or not, please stay safe and healthy, and practice physical distancing as part of fighting the COVID-19 pandemic. Listen to the medical professionals, and help them do their jobs. If [I]PI:E[/I] can teach the general public anything, it would be that behaving otherwise can lead to scenarios that are much scarier and deadlier.

So what is the game about, and why are so many people offended by it?

Well, in the game, you get to roleplay an innocent little bacteria, or virus, or other "germ" who has no idea what a human is, and you get to mutate the little germ in such a way that, by pure coincidence, all of humanity is wiped off the face of the earth.

There is something very eye-opening, that moment when the last remaining humans on the planet realize the time of man has come to an end.  It is really quite startling to imagine such a time as a possibility.

Gameplay elements consist of:

- Initial creation of the germ (as a bacteria, virus or whatever else you have unlocked)

- Initial placement of the first infection in a certain country

- As the infection spreads from human to human, and from country to country, popups appear on the map that you can pop, which provide mutation points which you can invest into changing the germ to be more infectious, or more deadly, or even less deadly if you think that will help your innocent agenda as a germ

- As humans become aware of your existence, they will try to come up with a vaccine to cure themselves against you.  This is what you are doing all you can to prevent.

- The biggest benefit of playing this game, is that it gives an educational backdrop to properly protecting ourselves against plagues - which even in modern days have the real danger of wiping out humanity.

But is it realistic?  Well I hate to pop anyone's bubble, but the game-play does assume that once a person is infected, they remain infected for life, and that genetic mutations will happen across the population uniformly, to provide that last fatal blow to humanity.  But this is not how genetic mutations work - various strains of a virus come in small pockets.

For example, you can look at all the strains of COVID-19 out in the wild today, at this nice website:
https://nextstrain.org/ncov?c=clade_membership&fbclid=IwAR2IuoJbNvKtoSAACgp6CufvTb3nTQG16V8Gn50KMG56ka432A7N6Vu0jhc

Is the game fun?

Obviously if you don't like the idea of wiping out humanity, that might put a damper on your enjoyment.  But I don't think of it like that - I think of it as a real possibility, and the game provides some idea of just how difficult it would be (i.e. just how astronomically unlucky humanity would have to be for such a perfect storm to happen).  The game is fantastic and worth everyone giving it a try.

Now that the multiplayer update is out, I figured I would go ahead and make a review of the game, now that it's mostly completed. The short answer: If you like strategy games, or are fascinated by the idea of creating your own pathogen to destroy humanity, buy this game, especially during a sale.

The details:

The base game is a genetic strategy game where your goal is to infect the world and destory it before they can do the same to you. It offers plenty of options for doing so, and the game is simple enough in the lower difficulties for newcomers to get a basic idea of what to do, but in harder difficulties, it is challenging enough for even veteran players to have a difficult challenge. The game has many different plague types and modes to try, including user created plagues.

The multiplayer mode is also fun, sporting many strategies that counter other strategies, with quite a bit of depth. Would advise AGAINST newcomers to the game from playing that mode first, as it is much more intense of an experience compared to the main game.  Against friends or randoms, the multiplayer is a great addition to an already great game.

I've played this game ever since 2012, whenever the game first started out on mobile devices and there was only 6 plagues and 3 difficulties. This game has kept my attention and still manages to be a fun distraction and experience to come back to time and time again. So, if you seem at all interested, pick it up, it's a strategy game that's worth the price.

Plague Inc.: Evolved; let me first start out by saying, this is exactly how the Early Access model should be done. This game is an absolute treat to play.

The main idea behind the game, if you don't already know (I’d be surprised if you didn't to be honest), is to develop, mutated and transmit your very own disease. You can choose which symptoms you would like your diseases to have, how you would like it to be transmitted around the world and many other different options. There are a number of different kinds of diseases you can choose, my favourite has to be the zombie plague; each of the different modes offers different symptoms, abilities and ways to transmit your creation as well. 

The graphics are essentially a 2D world map; you don't need anything else for this game, the UI and HUD are very nicely put together and you can get all of the information you require within a key press. 

Each of the different modes have been carefully crafted so that no game ever feels the same; this game really makes you think, would this symptom thrive in these conditions? How can I get my plague to travel to the other side of the world when all of the airports are closed? The possibilities are endless. 

The game can also vary in difficulty; each different mode has 4 stages of difficulty; and boy oh boy does it get hard in the brutal stages. You are best of cracking out a guide if you want to tackle some of the harder stages.

I have played about ten hours so far; this has enabled me to complete all the different types of diseases and modes on offer, done a couple on Brutal difficulty and worked on a few achievements. There are still roughly 100 more achievements to collect along with the scenario modes to play; and given that they game is still in early access, I fully expect there to be more content added soon too. 

I can 100% guarantee that anyone will enjoy this game; it’s a perfect pick up and play game but you can also get mind numbingly deep into the inner workings of diseases and plagues without having to do six years in medical school.

If you found this review helpful, please consider giving it a thumbs up. You can also find more reviews over at http://www.completingthebackloggroup.com/
